issues.legal_issue: The limitation period for a transferee to perfect title by adverse possession over granted land transferred in breach of a grant condition depends on whether the grant conveyed ownership to the grantee or merely allotted possession while retaining the State’s title.
material_facts: The original grantee received the land subject to a 15-year restriction on transfer, but transferred part of it in breach of that restriction before the Act came into force.
The appellant later acquired the land and claimed to have perfected title through more than 12 years of continuous adverse possession before the Act came into force.

The Assistant Commissioner declared the transfer void and ordered restoration, and the High Court rejected the adverse-possession claim by applying a 30-year period without examining the grant deed to determine whether ownership had passed to the original grantee.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s order was set aside and the matter was remanded for examination of the grant deed and other relevant material to determine whether the grant transferred ownership or was only an allotment. An absolute grant is subject to the ordinary 12-year period, while an allotment that leaves title with the State is subject to the 30-year period. The claimant bears a heavy burden to establish that title was extinguished before the Act commenced, and the court must consider whether the claim was raised at the earliest opportunity and what supporting material was then produced.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(b), 4 and 5 of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978, a transfer in breach of a grant condition is ordinarily void and may lead to resumption and restoration. Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka read the Act to exclude a transfer made before commencement where the transferee had already perfected title by prescription. Sunkara Rajayalakshmi v. State of Karnataka clarified that the 30-year period running against the State applies where the State retained title; it does not displace the ordinary 12-year period where the grant transferred absolute ownership. The character of the grant must be determined from the evidence in each case.

rule.if: restoration_appeal and pre_commencement_breach_transfer and adverse_possession_claim and grant_character_unresolved

predicates.restoration_appeal: The proceeding challenges a decision to resume or restore land transferred in breach of a grant condition.
predicates.pre_commencement_breach_transfer: The land was transferred in breach of a grant condition before the protective restoration law commenced.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: The transferee claimed to have perfected title through continuous adverse possession before that law commenced.
predicates.grant_character_unresolved: The available decision did not establish whether the grant conveyed ownership or merely allotted possession while title remained with the State.

issues.definition: When a restoration appeal involves a pre-commencement breach transfer and a claim of prior adverse possession, the court must establish whether the grant conveyed ownership or retained title in the State before selecting the applicable limitation period.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant whose possession or tenancy rights may be affected by a decision in a title dispute must be treated as an interested party and given notice and an opportunity to be heard in the statutory revision proceeding.
material_facts: The appellants claimed to occupy disputed land as tenants under leases granted by the Gram Panchayat, including annual leases or pattas.

In proceedings brought by persons claiming ownership, the Director decided a title dispute between those claimants and the Gram Panchayat and ordered distribution of the land without hearing the appellants.
The decision could affect the appellants’ possession or tenancy rights, and they claimed that they remained in possession as tenants.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were interested parties entitled to notice and an opportunity to be heard before an order was passed. The orders were set aside and the matters remanded for fresh consideration after hearing the appellants and other necessary parties, including consideration of whether any appellants remained in possession as tenants and how their rights could be protected.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 makes notice and an opportunity to be heard conditions precedent to varying or reversing an order for parties interested. A person is interested if likely to be affected by the decision. The court relied on Northern India Caterers P. Ltd. v. State of Punjab and Haryana and Mohan Lal v. State of Punjab on lawful process and hearing; Paras Ram v. State of Punjab and Gram Panchayat of Village Serohi Behali v. Har Lal on the broad meaning of interested parties; and Mukhtiar Singh v. State of Punjab and Chet Singh v. State of Punjab on the statutory requirement for a hearing under Section 42.

predicates.section_42_revision: The proceeding is a statutory revision concerning an order, scheme, or repartition in a land-consolidation matter.
predicates.tenant_claims_interest_in_land: A person claims to hold a tenancy or leasehold interest in the land under consideration.
predicates.decision_may_affect_tenancy_or_possessio: The decision may adversely affect that person's tenancy rights or possession of the land.

issues.definition: In a land-consolidation revision, a person claiming a tenancy interest must be heard when the decision may affect that person's tenancy rights or possession.
